a: He had already been king over Greece
p: Venetus reads 'the first' over Greece, as the KJV and Vulgate take it; Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus read 'formerly.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus agrees
readings.plain: He had already been king over Greece

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("the first over Greece") and the Vulgate (qui primus regnavit in Graecia) give this sense
readings.plain: He was the first king over Greece

why: The adverb of Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus is the better-supported reading. The history fits either: Alexander led the Greeks before he took Persia, and he was also the first king of the Greek empire. Venetus's adjective makes him the first king of the Greek empire. See the note.

p: Alexandrinus says 'they gave them authority'; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV say the king gave it.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("who gave them licence") and the Vulgate (dedit) follow this text

why: The sense is the same: the authority came from the king's government. The Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus's plural with an English passive.

a: And they committed a massacre and spoke with great arrogance
p: Alexandrinus makes the massacre and the boasting plural; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV give both to the king.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἐποίησαν φονοκτονίαν, καὶ ἐλάλησαν ὑπερηφανίαν μεγάλην
readings.en: and they made a massacre and spoke great arrogance
readings.plain: And they committed a massacre and spoke with great arrogance

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (fecit, locutus est) follow this text
readings.en: and he made a massacre and spoke great arrogance
readings.plain: And he committed a massacre and spoke with great arrogance

why: The singular is smoother, since Antiochus is the subject of the sentence, and scribes may have made the verbs agree with him. Alexandrinus's plural, the king and his troops, is the harder reading.

p: A corrector of Alexandrinus wrote 'the sanctuary' over an erasure where the first hand had 'the Sabbath.'

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, Codex Venetus (V; the digital apparatus prints it as a Greek Α), and Alexandrinus as first written, apparently (A*vid)
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), a corrector writing over an erasure, from Swete's apparatus

why: Swete prints "the Sabbath" from Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus's first hand. The KJV and the Vulgate (sabbatum) agree. The corrector may have been thinking of 1:37 or 1:46, where the sanctuary is profaned.

p: For 'common' (unclean) animals, Sinaiticus first wrote 'many'; a corrector made it 'new.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV ("unclean beasts") and the Vulgate (pecora communia) agree
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, as first written (ℵ*)
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, a corrector (ℵc.a)

why: "Common" in the sense "ritually unclean" is the usage of 1:62 and of Mark 7:2 and Acts 10:14. The other readings are scribal slips between similar Greek words.

a: and also their families and those who had circumcised them
p: Alexandrinus has no verbs here. A corrector of Sinaiticus adds 'plundered' and 'killed,' as the KJV has.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ τοὺς οἰκείους αὐτῶν, καὶ τοὺς περιτετμηκότας αὐτούς
readings.en: and their households, and those who had circumcised them
readings.plain: and also their families and those who had circumcised them

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, as first written, and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD)
readings.en: and their houses, and those who had circumcised them
readings.plain: and also their houses and those who had circumcised them

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, a corrector (ℵc.a), who reads "houses" with the first hand and adds the two verbs; the KJV ("rifled their houses, and slew them") follows a text like this
readings.orig: οικους ℵV αυτων 2⁰] + προενομευσαν ℵc.a αυτους] + εθανατωσαν ℵc.ᵃ
readings.en: and they plundered their houses, and they killed those who had circumcised them
readings.plain: and they plundered their houses and killed those who had circumcised them

why: The short text is abrupt, and the corrector's verbs look like an attempt to fill it out. The Vulgate (per universas domos eorum ... trucidabant) fills it differently, which suggests that each tradition was repairing the same gap.

p: Alexandrinus says many in Israel 'were hanged.' Sinaiticus and Venetus say they 'held strong,' which fits the verse.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("were fully resolved") and the Vulgate (definierunt) give this sense

why: The Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus here. Its "were hanged" seems to have been drawn in from "they hung" in 1:61, and it does not fit what follows: these people "steeled themselves not to eat what was unclean" and chose to die (1:63).

p: The Greek codices call Jonathan Sapphus; the Latin and the KJV call him Apphus.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus
Latin Vulgate (Clementine edition); the KJV agrees

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Latin. The Greek name begins with the last letter of the word before it, "called" (kaloumenos), and the S was probably copied twice. The name is usually explained from Hebrew happus, "the cunning," or a word for "the beloved," which begin with a vowel.

p: The Greek says the Temple has become 'like a glorious man.' The Latin and the KJV read 'without honor.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading in ℵ or V
Latin Vulgate (Clementine edition); the KJV ("without glory") and the Douay ("without honour") give this sense

why: The Plain English Translation departs from all three Greek codices here. "Like a glorious man" contradicts the lament, which mourns that the Temple's glory is taken away (2:9). The Old Latin translation, which the Vulgate keeps unrevised in Maccabees, seems to have read a Greek word for "without honor" (adoxos), which differs from the codices' endoxos by a few letters; or the Greek once had a negative that dropped out. Many modern versions also translate "without honor." The source of the KJV's "without glory" is not identified.

p: Alexandrinus has 'the leaders of Judah'; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV have 'the men of Judah.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (viri Juda) follow this text

why: "The men of Judah" claims more: all Judah had given in. Either could be original; the Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus.

p: Alexandrinus has 'the king's law'; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV have 'the king's words.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (verba regis) follow this text

why: Alexandrinus sets "the king's law" against the law of God that Mattathias keeps (2:21), a sharp contrast that a scribe may have softened. The two words differ by a few letters in Greek.

p: Alexandrinus says the man came to burn incense; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV say to sacrifice.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("to sacrifice") and the Vulgate (sacrificare idolis, "to sacrifice to idols") follow this text

why: The two Greek words differ by two letters. The king's officer had asked for sacrifice (2:15, 25), which may have drawn the other reading in.

p: The KJV says Mattathias was zealous 'for the law of God.' The Greek says only 'for the law.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading
King James Version (1611); its source is not identified, and Swete's apparatus has no such Greek
readings.en: dealt zealously for the law of God
readings.plain: zealous for the law of God

why: The Vulgate (zelatus est legem) and the Douay also lack "of God." The KJV's addition makes explicit what the book leaves unsaid; 1 Maccabees avoids the word God throughout (see the note at 2:61).

p: Sinaiticus and Venetus read 'an assembly of Jews.' Alexandrinus, the KJV and the Vulgate name the Hasideans.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete (Alexandrinus spells it Asideōn)
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: the whole assembly of Jews, strong

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus, which also reads "the whole assembly" and has a different word for "strong"
readings.en: the whole assembly of Jews, strong

why: "Hasideans" is the harder reading: the name appears again at 7:13 and in 2 Maccabees 14:6, while "Jews" looks like a scribe's replacement for an unfamiliar name.

p: Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV promise 'an everlasting name' rather than 'everlasting glory.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (nomen aeternum) follow this text

why: Alexandrinus repeats "glory" for emphasis; the other reading avoids the repetition and echoes the "name" of 2:64 and 3:14. Both are possible.

p: Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV read 'an everlasting priesthood,' the words of Numbers 25:13.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: an inheritance of an everlasting covenant of priesthood
readings.plain: an inheritance of an everlasting covenant of priesthood

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (sacerdotii aeterni) give this sense

why: Numbers 25:13 promises Phinehas "a covenant of everlasting priesthood," and the other readings may have been made to agree with it. Alexandrinus's "holy" is the reading that does not match its source.

a: and he will not be found
p: Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV add 'tomorrow': 'today lifted high, tomorrow not found.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and he will not be found
readings.plain: and he will not be found

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (cras) follow this text
readings.en: and tomorrow he will not be found
readings.plain: and tomorrow he will not be found

why: The longer text gives a neat contrast and may be original, lost in Alexandrinus; or a scribe may have added the obvious word. The meaning is the same.

a: you will wage the war of the peoples
p: Alexandrinus says 'you will wage the war'; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV say Judas will.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: you will wage the war of the peoples

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("fight the battle of the people") and the Vulgate (ipse aget) give this sense
readings.plain: he will wage the war of the peoples

why: The sons are being told to follow Judas, so either fits. Alexandrinus makes the war the whole people's, under Judas's command.

p: Alexandrinus says they took the enemy's gear; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV say their spoils.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (spolia) follow this text

why: The two Greek words look alike. "Equipment" suits a band of rebels short of weapons (4:6) who arm themselves from the dead.

p: Alexandrinus misspells the pass as 'Methoron.' Sinaiticus and Venetus have Beth-horon.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (Bethoron) agree

why: The Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus here. Its M is a slip for the B of Beth-; at 3:24 Alexandrinus itself spells the name Bethoron (Swete's apparatus).

p: Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV read 'the God of heaven'; Alexandrinus has only 'Heaven.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (Dei caeli) follow this text

why: Elsewhere the book always says "Heaven" for God (3:50, 60; 4:10, 24, 55), so the shorter text fits its usage, and a scribe would more likely add "God" than remove it.

a: He will shatter them in front of us himself
p: The Vulgate and the KJV say 'the Lord himself.' The Greek says only 'he himself.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading here
readings.en: and he himself will crush them
readings.plain: He will shatter them in front of us himself

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine edition); the KJV ("the Lord himself") agrees
readings.en: the Lord himself will crush them
readings.plain: The Lord will shatter them in front of us himself

why: "He" refers back to Heaven (3:19). The Latin supplies the name the book avoids.

p: Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV add that he 'had outdone the kings before him' in giving.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("for he had abounded above the kings that were before him") and the Vulgate follow this text
readings.orig: + και επερισσευσεν υπερ τους βασιλεις τους εμπροσθεν ℵV
readings.en: with a generous hand, and he had outdone the kings before him
readings.plain: with an open hand, and he had outdone the kings before him

why: The addition matches Polybius's picture of Antiochus's lavish gifts, and could be original. The Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus's shorter text.

p: Venetus gives the army as fifty thousand foot soldiers.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV and the Vulgate agree
Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus

why: The other witnesses agree on forty. See the note on the size of the armies.

a: Let us raise up our people and our holy place from their ruin
p: Sinaiticus has a different second half: 'let us fight for our people and the holy place,' as the KJV has.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Ἀναστήσωμεν τὴν καθαίρεσιν τοῦ λαοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ τῶν ἁγίων
readings.en: let us raise up the ruin of our people and of the holy place
readings.plain: Let us raise up our people and our holy place from their ruin

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, as first written (ℵ*), which has these words in place of "and of the holy place"
readings.orig: πολεμησομεν περι ... του λαου ημων και των λαων
readings.en: let us raise up the ruin of our people, and let us fight for our people and the peoples
readings.plain: Let us raise up our people from their ruin, and let us fight for our people and the peoples

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, a corrector (ℵ¹, apparently), who changed "peoples" to "holy place"; the KJV ("Let us restore the decayed fortune of our people, and let us fight for our people and the sanctuary") and the Vulgate (pugnemus pro populo nostro, et sanctis nostris) follow this text
readings.en: let us raise up the ruin of our people, and let us fight for our people and the holy place
readings.plain: Let us raise up our people from their ruin, and let us fight for our people and the holy place

why: Swete's note means that Sinaiticus replaces "and of the holy place" with a new clause; it does not add a clause. In Sinaiticus the holy place moves from the first half to the second, and its first scribe miscopied it as "the peoples." The Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus.

p: The Vulgate and the KJV address God by name: 'unless thou, O God, help us.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading here
Latin Vulgate (Clementine edition); the KJV agrees

why: The Greek, like the rest of the book, does not use the word God.

a: whatever the will in Heaven is
p: The KJV and the Douay say 'the will of God ... in heaven.' The Greek and the Vulgate have only 'the will in heaven.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading here
readings.orig: ὡς δ᾽ ἂν ᾖ θέλημα ἐν οὐρανῷ
readings.en: as the will in heaven may be
readings.plain: whatever the will in Heaven is

readings.w: King James Version (1611) and the Douay (Challoner's revision, 1750); the Vulgate (voluntas in caelo) does not have "of God," and Swete's apparatus has no such Greek
readings.en: as the will of God is in heaven
readings.plain: whatever the will of God in Heaven is

why: Both English versions make explicit what the Greek leaves to "Heaven."

a: Perhaps he will want us still
p: The Vulgate and the KJV say 'the Lord will have mercy on us,' where the Greek says 'if he will want us.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading here
readings.plain: Perhaps he will want us still

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Clementine edition); the KJV ("if peradventure the Lord will have mercy upon us") gives this sense
readings.en: the Lord will have mercy on us
readings.plain: Perhaps the Lord will have mercy on us

why: The Greek thelein with a person, "to want, take pleasure in," is the Septuagint's idiom (Psalm 18:19, "since he took pleasure in me"; Psalm 17:20 in the Greek numbering). The Old Latin translation, which the Vulgate keeps unrevised in Maccabees, seems to render the sense freely and supply "the Lord."

p: Alexandrinus has 'the plains of Judea'; Sinaiticus and the KJV have 'the plains of Idumea.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Venetus agrees
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (Idumaeae) follow this text

why: Idumea lay to the south, far from the line of flight toward Gazara, Azotus and Jamnia in the west, so "Judea" (here the lowland of Judea) fits the geography better. The two names are easily confused; at 4:29 Sinaiticus makes the opposite swap. Neither is certain.

p: The Vulgate says they blessed 'God' toward heaven; the KJV says 'the Lord in heaven.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading of these words
Latin Vulgate (Clementine edition); the KJV ("praised the Lord in heaven") gives this sense

why: The Greek, "they blessed into heaven," uses Heaven for God, as the book does throughout.

a: For his loyal love is good forever
p: Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV have the full refrain of Psalm 136: 'for he is good, for his love is forever.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Ὅτι καλὸν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: for good forever is his mercy
readings.plain: For his loyal love is good forever

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV and the Vulgate (quoniam bonus est, quoniam in saeculum misericordia ejus) follow this text
readings.en: for it is good, for his mercy is forever
readings.plain: For it is good, for his loyal love is forever

why: The fuller text matches the psalm, and a scribe could have dropped a repeated "for"; it could also be a scribe's correction toward the familiar words. The Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus.

a: They took whole stones, as the law says, and built
p: Alexandrinus and Venetus say 'he took ... and he built.' Swete prints the plural from Sinaiticus.

readings.w: Swete's printed text: ἔλαβον from Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and ᾠκοδόμησαν from a corrector of it (ℵc.a); the KJV and the Vulgate (acceperunt, aedificaverunt) agree
readings.plain: They took whole stones, as the law says, and built

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: He took whole stones, as the law says, and built

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus, as first written (ℵ*)
readings.plain: They took whole stones, as the law says, and he built

why: Here Swete departs from Alexandrinus, and the Plain English Translation follows his printed text, with the KJV and the Vulgate. The case is not one-sided: Alexandrinus has singulars in 4:47–48 ("he took," "he built," "he consecrated") and again at 4:57, and may present Judas as the builder. At 4:48 and 4:57 the Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus's singular (see the 4:48 entry).

p: The KJV says they praised 'the God of heaven.' The Greek and the Vulgate have only 'heaven.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete reports no other reading of these words
King James Version (1611); its source is not identified, and Swete's apparatus has no such Greek

why: The Vulgate (benedixerunt in caelum) and the Douay ("blessed up to heaven") keep the Greek's reticence; the KJV supplies the name.

a: They shed innocent blood all around the sanctuary
p: Venetus reads 'the sanctuary of the Lord,' one of the few places where a witness of 1 Maccabees names God.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus agrees
readings.plain: They shed innocent blood all around the sanctuary

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus, which adds "of the Lord" (κυρίου, abbreviated)
readings.en: around the sanctuary of the Lord
readings.plain: They shed innocent blood all around the sanctuary of the Lord

why: Venetus alone adds the word, against Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus; the book elsewhere avoids naming God (see the note at 2:61).

a: at the windows of the houses
p: Alexandrinus says incense was burned at the windows of the houses; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV say at the doors.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: at the windows of the houses
readings.plain: at the windows of the houses

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("at the doors of their houses") and the Vulgate (ante januas domorum) follow this text
readings.en: at the doors of the houses
readings.plain: at the doors of the houses

why: The two Greek words look alike, and doors seem the likelier place for an offering in the street. But Jeremiah tells of incense burned to other gods on roofs (Jeremiah 19:13), so an offering at a window is possible, and the Plain English Translation keeps Alexandrinus.

a: and he ordered them to be ready for a year for every need
p: Alexandrinus says 'for a year' twice: pay for a year, and readiness for a year. Sinaiticus and Venetus have it once.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἐνετείλατο αὐτοῖς εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν εἶναι ἑτοίμους εἰς πᾶσαν χρείαν
readings.en: and he ordered them to be ready for a year for every need
readings.plain: and he ordered them to be ready for a year for every need

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus, which lack the second "for a year"; the KJV ("commanding them to be ready whensoever he should need them") gives this sense
readings.en: and he ordered them to be ready for every need
readings.plain: and he ordered them to be ready for every need

why: The repeated phrase may be a scribe's echo of the first, or the original's stress on a year's campaign. The meaning hardly changes.

a: to root out and wipe out
p: Alexandrinus says 'to root out'; Sinaiticus has a word meaning 'to crush.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV ("to destroy and root out") gives this sense
readings.plain: to root out and wipe out

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.orig: και του εκτριφαι ℵ [sic, for ἐκτρῖψαι]
readings.plain: and to crush and wipe out

why: The words differ by one letter in Greek. Alexandrinus's "root out" fits the plan to resettle the land (3:36).

p: Alexandrinus has a form that would mean 'who have seen your name'; Sinaiticus, Venetus and the KJV have 'who know.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: those who have seen your name
readings.plain: all who have seen your name

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("all those that know thy name") follows this text

why: The Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus here. "Those who know your name" is a phrase of the Psalms (Psalm 9:10), and in the Greek of this period ei and i sounded alike, so Alexandrinus's spelling is probably a slip for the same word.

p: Alexandrinus says 'he consecrated the courts'; Sinaiticus says 'they consecrated.'

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("and hallowed the courts") and the Vulgate (sanctificaverunt) give the plural sense

why: The singular is Alexandrinus's, and the Plain English Translation keeps it; see the note on who is meant.
